I will use an example to make my case, but it should be clear that the reasoning (if my explanation is clear enough) can readily be generalized.

 

Suppose you are a carpenter. You use various tools to help you in your work, one of these tools being a plane. I happen to want a plane, and I offer you this deal: I will borrow the plane for one year, and return it to you at the end of the year. I promise to return it in good condition. Supposing further that you can rely on me to keep my promise - would you agree to the deal?

I don't think you would agree to it (unless you had some special reason for wanting to do a favor for me). The reason is that the deal is a pure loss to you: you lose something of value to you for a year, and afterward you only get back what you would otherwise have had all along.

So (even in a barter economy) I would have to offer you something else, in addition to the return of the plane itself, to compensate you for being deprived of the use of the plane for one year.

Having the plane now really is of greater value than the prospect of having the plane one year from now. That's why the interest return beyond the amount lent ("the amount lent" being the plane itself) is justified.

 

(My example is based on one used by the 19th century French economist, Frederic Bastiat, in his essay "Capital and Interest".)

Capitalism

The socio-economic system where social relations are based on commodities for exchange, in particular private ownership of the means of production and on the exploitation of wage labour.

Wage labour is the labour process in capitalist society: the owners of the means of production (the bourgeoisie) buy the labour power of those who do not own the means of production (the proletariat), and use it to increase the value of their property (capital). In pre-capitalist societies, the labour of the producers was rendered to the ruling class by traditional obligations or sheer force, rather than as a “free” act of purchase and sale as in capitalist society.
